h1: Starting a homebrew club in your city and keeping it going
title: Starting and Running a Homebrew Club | Craft Beer School
desc: How to start a homebrew club in an Indian city, run meetings people come back to, swap beer fairly and keep it alive past the first year.
teaser: Most homebrew clubs die in month four. Here is what the ones that last do differently.
standfirst: A homebrew club is the fastest way to get better at brewing, because other people will taste your beer honestly. Starting one is easy. Keeping it going takes a few simple habits that we have seen work again and again.
sections: Why a club beats brewing alone

Brewing alone, you are the only judge of your beer. You drank it, you liked it, you moved on. A club changes that. Ten people taste your pale ale and two of them say the same thing: a bit of green apple, a slightly thin finish. That is information you could not get from a recipe forum.

Clubs also share the boring costs. A sack of base malt split five ways is easier to store and cheaper per kilo than buying small packs. One member owns a grain mill, another has a spare chest freezer, someone else knows how to keg. Problems that take a beginner six months to solve get solved over one evening.

You need fewer people than you think. Five regular brewers is a club. Fifteen who turn up once is a mailing list.

Start where homebrewers already are: the WhatsApp groups run by ingredient suppliers, Instagram accounts posting brew day photos from your city, people who bought starter kits from the same shop. A short message works better than a poster: "Starting a monthly homebrew meet in Pune. Bring a beer you made, good or bad. First one on Sunday at 5."

The phrase "good or bad" matters. Beginners stay away if they think everyone else is brewing perfect IPAs. Say clearly that faulty beer is welcome because faulty beer is where the learning is.
Where to meet and what to keep in mind

A member's terrace, a co-working space after hours or a friendly brewpub on a slow weekday all work. Some brewpubs like hosting clubs because the members are exactly the people who buy their beer later. Ask first. Offer to keep it small.

A word on rules. The legal position on homebrewing in India is unclear in many states and selling homebrew without a licence is not allowed anywhere we know of. Keep the club strictly non-commercial: no selling beer, no entry fee that looks like a ticket for drinks, no members under the legal drinking age for your state. Rules vary by state and change, so if the club grows large or runs public events, check the current position with a local licensing consultant.
A meeting format people come back for

Clubs fade when meetings turn into an unstructured drinking session. Give each one a spine:

  1. A theme. One style a month, one ingredient, or one fault. "Everyone brews a saison" gives you six versions of the same beer to compare, which teaches more than six random bottles.
  2. A short talk. Ten minutes from a member on something they learned: water salts, yeast starters, how they built a fermentation chamber.
  3. Structured tasting. Pour small samples of 50 to 60 ml each. Score them on a simple sheet. Our guide to setting up a beer tasting has a format that works.
  4. Open bottles last. Social time after the scoring, not before, so palates are fresh when it counts.

Keep pours small and the evening short. People should leave able to remember the feedback they got. Make sure there is water, food and a lift home for anyone who needs one.
Getting beer to the meeting in good shape

In Indian weather this is the step that ruins feedback. A bottle-conditioned beer carried across the city in an auto at 34 °C arrives warm, foamy and tasting worse than it did at home. The fix is a cooler box with ice packs and a rule that bottles go into it straight from the fridge. Ask members to bring 330 ml bottles rather than litre swing-tops, so nobody opens a big bottle for six small pours.

Label every bottle with the style, original and final gravity, yeast and the date it was packaged. Without those details, feedback stays vague. With them, someone can say "that finished at 1.016, so your mash was probably too hot" and be right.
Keeping it alive after the first year

Most clubs stall when the founder gets busy. Spread the work early. Rotate who hosts, who picks the theme and who runs the scoring sheet. Keep a shared document of every beer tasted, with scores and notes, so the club has a memory and new members can see what has been tried.

Give the year some goals. A group brew day where everyone works one batch together. A club entry into a competition: our guide to entering a homebrew competition covers how judging works. An off-flavour night where you spike a neutral beer with common faults and learn to name them.

Somewhere in that first year, a few members will want to go deeper than club evenings allow: why a mash at 68 °C gives a fuller beer than one at 64 °C, or how to read a fermentation properly. That is the point where structured learning helps. It is also where a club full of people who brew together becomes a club that brews well.
faqs: How many people do I need to start a homebrew club?
Five regular brewers is enough. A small group that meets every month and brings beer each time does more than a large group that rarely shows up.
Is it legal to run a homebrew club in India?

The position on homebrewing is unclear in many states and selling homebrew without a licence is not allowed. Keep the club non-commercial and check current rules with a local licensing consultant before running public events.
How should a homebrew club taste beer?
Pour small samples of about 50 ml, score them on a simple sheet and give specific feedback before any open social drinking. Label each beer with its style, gravities and yeast.
How do we stop the club from fading out?
Rotate the hosting and organising, set a theme for each meeting and keep a shared record of every beer tasted. Clubs fade when one person does everything.
